passage:
Saturday, late
Got the fourth internship rejection today. I turned it into a bit at dinner: "At this rate I'll be interning in my own bedroom." Everyone laughed. I did three more jokes on the walk back, one about framing the rejection emails. Sangeeta laughed at the first two, then went quiet. In our room she sat on the end of my bed and said, "You've been funny all day. How are you actually?" My throat closed up. I said, "Fine, obviously, I'm a comedian now," and she didn't laugh. She just waited. Then I cried for the first time since the first rejection. Turns out the jokes were holding the door shut. We talked for an hour. She said her cousin had found the careers cell useful, and I've booked a slot for Monday. I still think the bedroom-internship line was good. But I'm glad someone didn't laugh.
Aadhya

qa.q: When did Aadhya first joke about interning in a bedroom?
qa.a: At dinner.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling beneath the jokes?
qa.a: Aadhya felt hurt and discouraged by four rejections; the jokes eased the tension but held back distress that came out as tears once Sangeeta asked.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta's approach get right?
qa.a: She stopped laughing, asked a direct and serious question, waited through the deflecting joke, then listened and pointed toward the careers cell.

qa.q: How might the friends at dinner have seen Aadhya?
qa.a: As cheerful and coping well, since the jokes made them laugh, without realising how discouraged Aadhya felt.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult using jokes to ease the stress of rejections, and a friend seeing that constant joking may hide distress that deserves a serious talk.

passage:
Dear Tanvir,
I owe you a straight answer. When you asked last month what I was up to, I said I was "between jobs, exploring options." The truth is the company let me go in March, along with thirty others. I used the soft words because I was embarrassed, and because Ammi prefers them. Soft words are fine for some things. But I keep thinking about Nana's hospital stay. Everyone told you it was "a small check-up" so you wouldn't worry during exams, and you didn't come until the weekend. It was a heart scare. You were hurt that nobody said so, and you were right to be. So here's my rule now: gentle words for small things, clear words for health, safety and anything that needs a decision. I was laid off. I'm applying everywhere. I'm okay, mostly. And if I'm ever not okay, I'll say that plainly too.
Your cousin,
Rafiq

qa.q: When did the company let Rafiq go?
qa.a: In March, along with thirty others.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq use the words "between jobs"?
qa.a: Rafiq felt embarrassed about being laid off, and the soft phrase also suited Ammi's preference.

qa.q: What rule has Rafiq settled on?
qa.a: Gentle words for small things, but clear words for health, safety and anything that needs a decision.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel about the "small check-up" wording?
qa.a: Tanvir felt hurt that nobody told the truth about the heart scare, since the soft words kept Tanvir away until the weekend.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult using euphemisms like "between jobs" out of tact, and seeing how soft wording can blur meaning where health is concerned.

passage: The college photography exhibition closed in fifteen minutes, and the hall was packed and noisy with students hurrying to vote. Yogesh stopped in front of one print: a single clay lamp glowing on a dark windowsill. "Easy," he said. "Hope. Diwali. Light beating the darkness." Anirban frowned. "I see the opposite. When my grandfather died, we kept a lamp burning like that for days. To me it's mourning." They stood there arguing over the noise until the photographer, Mei, an exchange student from Kyoto, came to straighten the frame. "You're both a little right," she laughed. "I took it thinking of Obon, when we light lanterns to welcome our ancestors home. It's remembering, but warm, not only sad." Yogesh looked at the lamp again. The same flame had held three meanings in three minutes. With the closing bell ringing, he wrote on his voting slip: "Lamp: it means what you bring to it." Anirban voted for it too.

qa.q: Where was Mei an exchange student from?
qa.a: Kyoto.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel about his first reading once Mei explained?
qa.a: Yogesh felt surprised and less certain, seeing that his confident "easy" reading of hope was only one informed guess.

qa.q: What does this scene suggest about reading symbols in art?
qa.a: Treat a reading as an informed guess shaped by one's own culture and faith, and ask the maker or others where possible.

qa.q: How did Anirban see the lamp, and why?
qa.a: As mourning, because his family kept a lamp burning for days after his grandfather died.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult reading a lamp as a symbol and learning that its meaning varies by culture and religion, so interpretations are informed guesses.

passage: In the small church at Kuttanad, the harvest thanksgiving always fell in the week after the paddy was cut. Joseph, home from college, carried the first bundle of rice from his family's field up the aisle, the stalks scratching his arms, and laid it at the altar beside bananas and a jackfruit from someone's yard. His father had worked this field for thirty years, and this year the rains had nearly ruined it. When the choir began to sing, Joseph found his eyes stinging. Afterwards his friend Deepak, who had come along, said quietly, "At home we offer the first rice too, and light a lamp. Amma does it before anyone eats." Joseph nodded. "Different words, same thing." That evening they walked to Deepak's house, where Deepak's mother was setting a small brass lamp in front of a banana leaf of new rice. Joseph stood with folded hands while it was lit, quiet, feeling it.

qa.q: What did Joseph carry up the aisle?
qa.a: The first bundle of rice from his family's field.

qa.q: What did Joseph's stinging eyes during the singing suggest?
qa.a: He was moved and grateful, likely thinking of his father's thirty years on the field and how close the rains had come to ruining this harvest.

qa.q: How did Joseph and Deepak show respect for each other's rites?
qa.a: Deepak came to the church thanksgiving, and Joseph stood quietly with folded hands at the lamp-lighting, seeing them as "different words, same thing".

qa.q: How might Deepak's mother see the offering of new rice?
qa.a: As a way of giving thanks before anyone eats, a ritual of gratitude woven into her home.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult offering thanks through a harvest thanksgiving and a lamp with the first rice, showing ritual gratitude that varies by tradition.

subtype: Touching elders' feet and seeking blessings [Mismatch]
passage:
Anand: quick q before tomorrow's Dussehra lunch at your place
Anand: do I have to touch your Nani's feet? we don't really do that in my family and I don't want to get it wrong
Kalyani: good question! you don't have to
Kalyani: for me it's a way of asking for blessings and I like doing it. but it's not everyone's thing
Anand: won't she be offended?
Kalyani: Nani cares more about whether you eat three helpings 😄
Kalyani: a namaste and "happy Dussehra, Nani" is lovely. if you do it, do it because you want to, not because you're scared
Anand: okay. might try it if it feels right in the moment
Kalyani: perfect. my cousin Neel never does it and Nani adores him
(next evening)
Anand: I did it! she put her hand on my head and said something in Marathi
Kalyani: she said "live long and eat well" 🙂 very her

qa.q: What did Nani do when Anand touched her feet?
qa.a: She put her hand on Anand's head and said something in Marathi.

qa.q: What was Anand worried about before the lunch?
qa.a: Anand felt anxious about getting it wrong and offending Nani, since touching feet isn't done in Anand's family.

qa.q: How did Kalyani help Anand choose?
qa.a: By explaining what the gesture means to Kalyani, saying it's optional, suggesting a namaste instead, and encouraging a choice made freely, not out of fear.

qa.q: How did Nani seem to receive Anand's gesture?
qa.a: Warmly: she blessed Anand with a hand on the head and a wish to "live long and eat well".

grounding: It illustrates that touching elders' feet signals respect in many Indian families but is not universal, and is best done by choice.

passage: At the government college in Solapur, the new interpreter, Mrs Kale, sat beside the blackboard every morning, signing the lectures for Vishal, who was Deaf and the first student there to have one. On Monday, during group work, Deepika turned to Mrs Kale and said, "Ask him if he's done the chemistry assignment." Mrs Kale signed it, and Vishal replied, but his eyes stayed on Deepika, a little flat. Later Mrs Kale took Deepika aside. "Speak to him, not to me. Say 'Have you done it?' and look at him. I'll carry the words." On Thursday Deepika tried. She faced Vishal, asked her question, then waited while Mrs Kale's hands caught up. The pause felt long, three or four seconds, and she almost repeated herself. She didn't. Vishal answered, grinning, and added a joke that took Mrs Kale a moment to translate. When the laugh finally reached Deepika, it landed just as warmly.

qa.q: Who was the interpreter?
qa.a: Mrs Kale.

qa.q: What might Vishal's flat look on Monday suggest?
qa.a: He likely felt talked about rather than talked to, a little hurt or left out, when Deepika addressed the interpreter; it could also have been simple tiredness.

qa.q: What did Deepika change on Thursday?
qa.a: She faced Vishal, spoke to him directly, and waited through the interpreter's lag instead of repeating herself.

qa.q: How did Mrs Kale see her own role?
qa.a: As someone who carries the words rather than a partner in the conversation, which is why she asked Deepika to speak to Vishal.

grounding: It illustrates a hearing student learning to speak to a Deaf classmate rather than to the interpreter, and to wait for the interpreter's lag.

subtype: Use of space and classifiers in sign [Interpreting]
passage: I go to the Saturday sign language club with Jasleen, so I saw her breakthrough. Avni, who is Deaf and runs the club, was telling us about a scooter crash she'd seen outside the market. Jasleen and I had been learning single signs for weeks, and at first we both kept trying to catch each one, like vocabulary cards. We were lost. Then Jasleen stopped squinting at Avni's fingers and sat back. Avni had put the scooter on her right and a cow on her left, in the air in front of her. One flat hand became the scooter, sliding forward; her other hand, a different shape, was the cow stepping out. When the hands met, Avni's face showed the shock, eyebrows up, cheeks puffed. Jasleen whispered, "The cow walked into it from the side." Avni saw, grinned and nodded. I can't say what finally made it click. But after that Jasleen watched the whole space, not just the hands, and so did I.

qa.q: Where did the scooter crash happen?
qa.a: Outside the market.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel before the story clicked?
qa.a: Jasleen felt lost and frustrated, squinting at single signs, until watching the whole space brought the relief of understanding.

qa.q: What changed Jasleen's understanding?
qa.a: Watching the whole signing space, where Avni placed the scooter and the cow, how the hand shapes moved and her face, instead of isolated signs.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when Jasleen whispered the right reading?
qa.a: Pleased, grinning and nodding that a learner had followed the story the way it was told 😊

grounding: It illustrates how a signer uses space and hand shapes to show who did what, and how watching the whole signing space rather than single signs gives the meaning.

passage: Vijay had twelve minutes before the hostel Wi-Fi shut off at midnight, and two messages to send. The first was to Ujjwal: "bro can u bring my charger to lab tmrw, dying here 😩". Easy. The second was to Professor Rao, asking for an extension on the thermodynamics assignment because his grandmother was in hospital. His thumbs, still in chat mode, typed: "hi sir can i get 2 more days for assgnmt, family thing." He stared at it. That was how he'd talk to Ujjwal, not to someone grading his work. With nine minutes left, he deleted it and started again: "Dear Professor Rao, I am writing to request a two-day extension for Assignment 3. My grandmother was admitted to hospital on Monday, and I have been with her. I will submit by Friday. Thank you for considering this. Regards, Vijay Kumar, Roll No. 42." He sent it with a minute to spare. At eight the next morning the reply came: "Granted. I hope she recovers soon."

qa.q: By which day did Vijay promise to submit?
qa.a: By Friday.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when he stared at the first draft?
qa.a: He felt uneasy that the chatty tone would seem careless or disrespectful to someone grading his work.

qa.q: What made the second email suit its reader?
qa.a: A formal greeting, a clear request with the reason, a firm new deadline, thanks, and his full name and roll number.

qa.q: How might Professor Rao have read the first draft if it had been sent?
qa.a: As rushed and casual, which could have made the request seem less serious.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult adjusting register between a text to a friend and an email to a professor, using greeting, courtesy and length to fit the relationship.

passage: You asked how I finally finished my personal statement, Jaya, so here's the confession. I'm Francis, and my first draft was full of words like "passionate", "hardworking" and "committed to excellence". My cousin read it and said, "This could be anybody. Where are you?" Fair. So I started again with something true: the summer I spent fixing the broken hand pump in my grandmother's village, taking it apart three times, getting it wrong twice, while the neighbours brought me tea and watched me fail. That's why I want to study water engineering. I also wrote about switching streams in second year, which I'd been hiding because it felt like failure. What I left out: my terrible cooking, my fear of public speaking, the months I spent doubting everything. It's not a lie. It's a window, not the whole house. The admissions office only sees the window. I just wanted it to be a real one.

qa.q: What did Francis spend a summer fixing?
qa.a: The broken hand pump in the grandmother's village.

qa.q: Why had Francis hidden the switch of streams at first?
qa.a: Francis felt ashamed of it, seeing the switch as a failure.

qa.q: What made the second draft stronger?
qa.a: Honest, specific detail, such as the hand pump, getting it wrong twice and the switch of streams, instead of generic claims.

qa.q: How might an admissions reader see the statement?
qa.a: As a real glimpse of Francis, while still seeing only a curated window rather than the whole person.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult writing a personal statement where honest, specific detail convinces more than generic claims, while knowing it is curated self-presentation.

subtype: Reading tone in text without voice [Interpreting]
passage: Jin had spent two evenings designing the poster for the student film society in Toronto, and at 5:40 he sent it to Felix with a long message: three colour options, two fonts, a question about the date. At 5:52 the reply came: "Fine. Use the blue." That was all. No thanks, no exclamation mark. Jin read it on the subway and felt his chest tighten. Fine? After two evenings? He drafted a reply, "Sorry it wasn't good enough," then deleted it. Instead, when he got off at his stop, he called. Felix answered on the fourth ring, breathless, wind roaring behind him. "Jin! Sorry, I'm running for a bus. The poster's great, honestly, the blue one's perfect. I'll write properly tonight." That night a message came with three exclamation marks and a list of everything he loved about it. Jin laughed at himself. The reply had been as short as Felix's free moment.

qa.q: How many colour options did Jin send?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: What did Jin feel on reading "Fine. Use the blue."?
qa.a: Jin felt hurt and anxious, chest tightening, reading the short reply as cold after two evenings of work.

qa.q: What did Jin do instead of sending the drafted reply?
qa.a: He called Felix to check, which showed the short reply came from rushing, not displeasure.

qa.q: What was Felix's situation when he replied?
qa.a: He was running for a bus, so he typed the shortest possible answer, meaning it as approval.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult misjudging the tone of a brief message as cold, and checking with a call instead of replying to a guess.
